video_title: Rent Control, Socialism, and the Fight to Save New York City
gist: Manhattan Institute president Reihan Salam walks Anthony Pompliano through the mechanics of New York City's affordability crisis, arguing that 1961 downzoning plus the 2019 rent law made rent-stabilized multifamily uneconomic (owners are handing back keys), that $43,000-per-pupil schools and a 300,000-person city payroll deliver poor service because the system optimizes for employment, and that New York State's $268 billion budget has turned Medicaid into the region's real economic base. He then maps how the DSA — revived by Occupy and Bernie Sanders and now staffing Zohran Mamdani's City Hall — built a durable coalition on a deliberately ambiguous socialist brand, and warns that AI and Bitcoin anxiety is being repurposed as a vehicle for UBI and expropriation agendas.

themes.theme: NYC housing supply and the 2019 rent law

insights.claim: New York City's 1961 rezoning replaced a regime where six-story apartment buildings could be built almost anywhere with restrictive zoning designed to compete with the suburbs, and the city never course-corrected when it began growing again in the 1980s and 1990s — leaving a permanent structural under-supply of housing.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: The supply constraint is statutory and 60+ years old, so NYC rents stay structurally high regardless of who is mayor unless zoning itself is changed.

insights.claim: The 2019 New York rent law is the specific break point that turned expensive housing into an 'extremely intense emergency': it ended the 1990s vacancy-decontrol compromise that let owners raise rent enough to renovate a vacant unit, and made eviction of problematic tenants much harder.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Dates the impairment of NYC rent-stabilized multifamily to a single 2019 statute — a repeal or softening would be the catalyst to re-rate the asset class; no repeal means continued value erosion.
insights.quote: If a unit becomes vacant, you are not allowed to raise the rent enough to make it worth your while to fix it up.

insights.claim: Decades of rent control degraded NYC multifamily values so severely that some owners burned down their own buildings for insurance settlements, and the city ended up seizing buildings that could not pay property taxes — a precedent Salam invokes as the template for what the current cycle produces.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Historical base case for how a rent-controlled multifamily cycle ends: distress, abandonment, municipal seizure — the tail risk on NYC stabilized paper is total, not partial.
insights.quote: if you want to destroy a city, you know, the only thing more effective than carpet bombing is rent control

insights.claim: A multifamily investor-operator active on X reports that his peers are already handing back the keys on building after building in New York City, indicating lender takebacks are happening now rather than as a forecast.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Watch NYC rent-stabilized loan books at regional lenders and CMBS pools for accelerating handbacks — the distress is contemporaneous, not prospective.
insights.quote: my friends are handing back the keys on building after building after building

insights.claim: The oft-cited 11-12% return on rent-stabilized NYC buildings is exaggerated because it blends buildings that mix stabilized and market-rate units with buildings that are entirely stabilized; the fully-stabilized ones are 'barely keeping your head above water.'
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Underwrite NYC multifamily by stabilized-unit percentage, not portfolio averages — blended figures hide which buildings are already uneconomic.

insights.claim: Even at a genuine 11-12% return, running rent-stabilized buildings is unattractive because the operational burden (trash, vermin, painting, problem tenants) is far heavier than other ways to earn the same return — so capital simply exits rather than fights.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Risk-adjusted, NYC stabilized housing loses the competition for private capital; expect persistent under-investment and deferred maintenance regardless of headline cap rates.
insights.quote: There's a lot way, you know, much easier ways to make 11 or 12%.

insights.claim: The activist goal in NYC housing is explicitly 'decommodification' — moving buildings out of private hands into government or nonprofit ownership — but the operating economics do not change under nonprofit ownership, so the gap must be closed by taxpayer subsidy.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Any social-housing buildout in NYC is a future municipal budget liability, which is a credit consideration for NYC and NY State municipal bonds.
insights.quote: They literally use the language of decommodification.

insights.claim: The city's own record as landlord argues against public ownership: hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers live in public housing that is substandard and even dangerous, whereas handing seized buildings back to private landlords — often immigrants building wealth — was a documented success story.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: The empirical case for privatization of distressed housing stock; if NYC re-municipalizes buildings, expect the NYCHA outcome rather than the privatized outcome.

insights.claim: The landlord was chosen as the 'perfect enemy' for a winnable class war because in New York City even someone earning half a million dollars rents and resents their landlord — a coalition-building mechanic, not an economic argument.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Explains why anti-landlord policy has unusually broad electoral support in NYC and why it is unlikely to reverse on affordability evidence alone.

insights.claim: New York City systematically blocked Walmart and big-box retail from entering in the 1990s despite available strip-mall and industrial-zoned sites in the outer boroughs, and the requirement to be 'connected' to politicians and organized labor functions as an extra tax on any retailer entering the city.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: A structural explanation for NYC's retail cost premium — and a reason national retailers' NYC unit economics differ from the rest of their footprint.
insights.quote: There was a systematic effort to prevent Walmart from coming to the city.

themes.theme: Cost-per-pupil versus outcomes in NYC schools

insights.claim: New York City spends roughly $43,000 per pupil in its public schools yet delivers lackluster educational performance, which Salam argues is not intrinsic because student achievement improved steadily under Mayor Bloomberg with fewer resources.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Per-pupil spending is not the binding constraint on outcomes — a spending-based political program in NYC should not be expected to move achievement.
insights.quote: we're spending $43,000 per pupil in the New York City public schools

insights.claim: NYC public schools deliver 120 fewer hours of instruction per year than the national average — against roughly 1,100 hours in a school year, that compounds to more than a full year of lost instruction across K-12, and NYC also trails its own charter schools on instructional hours.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: A hard, measurable input gap that explains outcome gaps better than funding does; charters' hour advantage is a durable performance edge.
insights.quote: we get 120 hours less than the national average

insights.claim: As families with young children leave New York City, schools with fewer than 150 pupils are kept open with full principal and assistant-principal staffing, because the system's organizing purpose has shifted from delivering a service to sustaining employment.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Enrollment decline in NYC will not produce cost savings — municipal education spending is sticky downward, a fiscal negative for the city's budget path.
insights.quote: there's this incredible machine that's built up over time that's a machine to extract

insights.claim: More than 100,000 NYC students are enrolled in charter schools and some NYC charters are the best school systems in the United States, but the political class refuses to grant additional charters to the highest-performing operators — Salam's read is that this protects the unionized workforce's market share.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: The charter cap is a political constraint on the only NYC education segment that works; a cap lift would be a genuine policy surprise worth tracking.
insights.quote: We are not going to give those operators that are crushing it. We are not going to give them more charters.

insights.claim: Union step-and-lane pay scales reward seniority and master's degrees rather than performance, pushing peak earnings decades out; since teachers improve most in their first five years and little between years 10 and 20, the structure drives young, hungry teachers out of the profession.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: A reusable model for why unionized labor markets lose their best young talent — and why competing charter networks can outbid on early-career pay.

insights.claim: Charter growth would be fiscally accretive to New York City because families with a credible school option stay and keep paying income, sales and property taxes — but the system optimizes for protecting the administrator class instead of the tax base.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Connects school policy directly to NYC's tax-base retention — the driver of municipal revenue and, downstream, city credit.

insights.claim: Pompliano proposes paying principals 50 cents of every dollar they save against their budget, conditioned on holding test-score performance, as a way to surface waste; Salam extends it to routing the surplus back to families as enrichment vouchers or college-savings contributions.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: A concrete incentive-design template for public-sector cost reduction that could be tested at district level anywhere.

themes.theme: Public safety staffing and the morale drain

insights.claim: The NYPD is below the headcount it needs, officers are working huge overtime, and Salam argues front-end compensation is inadequate to attract strong candidates — which forces weakened hiring standards and pushes experienced officers toward the exits.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Overtime-dependent staffing is a hidden municipal cost line and a leading indicator of a future public-safety deterioration in NYC.

insights.claim: Suburban departments and police forces in Texas and Florida are actively recruiting experienced NYPD officers with better pay and more respect, creating a one-way talent drain out of New York City.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Watch NYPD attrition and lateral-transfer data as a real-time gauge of NYC's public-safety trajectory — the input that historically drove NYC's real-estate and population cycles.
insights.quote: if you're an NYPD officer with some experience under your belt, I promise you there are uh police departments in Texas and Florida and all over the country that want you there

insights.claim: Homicides and shootings in New York City are improving, but Salam separates that from a distinct and unresolved 'disorder' problem and doubts the improvement is durable given staffing and morale conditions.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Headline violent-crime stats can stay good while the conditions that produce the next deterioration accumulate — do not read crime data alone as an all-clear on NYC.

insights.claim: Officers who arrest the same individual 14 times and see him back on the street the next day become demoralized, and the practical effect of a police force that doubts the city has its back is officers who do not rush in when danger appears.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: The transmission channel from bail/prosecution policy to actual street safety runs through officer discretion, not headcount alone — policy changes show up in behavior before they show up in statistics.

insights.claim: Salam's operating principle for public policy is to make government excellent only at what only government can do — armed forces, law enforcement, and the basic order that lets people raise families and build businesses.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: The filter he applies to every spending question; useful for anticipating Manhattan Institute positions on municipal budgets.
insights.quote: My core guiding principle is always let's make government excellent at what only government can do.

insights.claim: New York City employs over 300,000 people against a population of roughly 8.5 million, and visible disorder — graffiti, broken windows, accumulating trash — is what converts that headcount into taxpayer resentment because residents cannot see value for money.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: A 300k-person payroll is the fixed cost underneath NYC's budget; visible disorder is the political trigger that turns fiscal facts into taxpayer flight.
insights.quote: New York City employs over 300,000 people.

themes.theme: Medicaid as New York's real economic base

insights.claim: New York State spends $268 billion, with Medicaid at the center, and the federal government matches every state dollar — creating a structural incentive to spend more state money in order to draw down more borrowed federal dollars.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Any tightening of the federal Medicaid match is an outsized shock to New York State's budget and to the healthcare employment it underwrites.
insights.quote: New York State, you may have heard, spends $268 billion

insights.claim: The CDPAP consumer-directed home health aide program lets recipients hire their own daughter, son, or cousin as the paid caregiver with no meaningful verification of service delivery, and home health aide is simultaneously one of the fastest-growing jobs in New York City.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Fast job growth funded by an unverifiable benefit program is not real economic growth — discount NYC health-services employment gains accordingly.

insights.claim: Upstate New York's economy, once driven by manufacturing and tourism, is now anchored by state universities, state prisons and state hospital systems, with hospitals spending more money while serving fewer patients.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Upstate NY is effectively a government-transfer economy; regional banks and real estate there are exposed to state fiscal policy rather than private demand.
insights.quote: Now, you've got a lot of places in upstate New York that are supported by a state university or a state prison or a state hospital system where those hospitals are spending more and more money even though they have fewer and fewer patients.

insights.claim: Because so many nominally private-sector jobs in New York are funded by Medicaid dollars, the state has become what Salam calls an extraction environment, and job creators and investors read it as inhospitable and go elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Frames NY's business-climate problem as circular subsidy dependence rather than tax rates alone — a slower-moving but harder-to-reverse headwind.

insights.claim: New York has moved from merely permitting benefit collection to actively funding community organizers who knock on doors to enroll people, deliberately de-stigmatizing benefits — which Salam argues produces an entitlement mindset that changes immigrant assimilation outcomes.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Outreach-driven enrollment mechanically expands program caseloads and costs independent of underlying need — a budget dynamic that compounds.
insights.quote: we don't want to stigmatize, that's the word, we don't want to stigmatize collecting benefits

themes.theme: DSA machinery and the socialist brand

insights.claim: The DSA was founded in 1982 as a near-dead talking shop of anti-communist socialists, many of them passionate supporters of Israel, and was revived in the 2010s by Occupy Wall Street and the Bernie Sanders campaigns — meaning today's organization has almost nothing in common with its founding cohort.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: The DSA's radicalism is a 2010s phenomenon layered onto an old shell; its trajectory is set by the millennial cohort, not institutional history.

insights.claim: The DSA's core appeal to educated millennials was community rather than ideology — people who were not attending a synagogue, mosque, or church found a tight-knit group with a shared vision and a shared enemy.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Movements built on belonging are far stickier than movements built on policy; do not expect the DSA to dissolve when specific policies fail.

insights.claim: Only about 20% of children raised at the 90th income percentile end up at or above that percentile themselves, meaning roughly 80% of kids from affluent families experience downward mobility — the reservoir of frustration Salam says radical politics recruits from.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: A structural, demographic explanation for elite-educated radicalism that predicts the supply of recruits persists regardless of the economic cycle.
insights.quote: If your family was the 90th percentile, there's only a 20% chance you're at the 91st or 95th or 99th percentile yourself.

insights.claim: Socialism's power as a brand is precisely its ambiguity — it can mean clean Danish subways or the Bolivarian revolution in Venezuela — and Salam argues the DSA has successfully and deliberately blurred the two to widen its coalition.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Polling support for 'socialism' overstates support for its actual program; the gap is where political risk gets mispriced.
insights.quote: Now the beauty of socialism as a brand right now is actually that socialism can mean anything.

insights.claim: Mainstream Democratic members of Congress in New York already back Medicare for All variants and sit far to the left of Bill Clinton, so what now separates the DSA from the party mainstream is largely branding, aggression, and transgressiveness rather than policy substance.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Treating DSA-aligned candidates as a fringe underestimates the policy overlap already present in the mainstream party — the tail risk to markets is broader than the DSA label suggests.

insights.claim: The DSA cadre entering New York politics is disciplined, organized, highly capable and highly radical, and it is running up against a political establishment of time-servers that is not prepared for opponents like that.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Implies the socialist bloc in NYC governance is durable and likely to keep winning institutional fights — position for policy continuity, not reversion.
insights.quote: These are people who are disciplined, organized, highly capable, and highly radical.

insights.claim: The composition of New York City's newcomers flipped from roughly two-thirds immigrants and one-third college-educated professionals to the reverse, and while the white share of the population is roughly unchanged since 1990 at 30-35%, it is now transplants with no memory of pre-Giuliani New York rather than multi-generational Irish, Italian and Jewish outer-borough residents.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: The demographic mechanism behind NYC's political shift: an electorate with no lived memory of urban decline will not price the risk of policies that caused it.

insights.claim: The 2019 rent law was driven by people around current mayor Zohran Mamdani — including close adviser Cea Weaver, a leading tenant organizer — who did not live through the Bronx burning and the physical deterioration of NYC buildings.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Personnel continuity from the 2019 rent law into City Hall signals further housing-policy tightening rather than moderation.

themes.theme: AI, Bitcoin, and the narrative war for the rising generation

insights.claim: The shape of AI and Bitcoin is still being discerned, and Salam warns that people with pre-existing agendas — unconditional basic income, dramatic welfare-state expansion, expropriation of private property — are using anxiety and dread about these technologies as a vehicle to advance those agendas.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Expect AI-displacement anxiety to be converted into redistribution policy proposals; that is the political risk channel for tech and crypto holdings, not the technology itself.
insights.quote: there are a lot of people who already had a pre-cooked pre-existing agenda where they're using this and they're using the anxiety and dread around these new technologies as a vehicle to drive forward their pre-existing agenda

insights.claim: Salam explicitly reframes the fight over AI, crypto and capitalism as not right-versus-left but as competing narratives for winning the rising generation — and says the pro-building narrative currently has no one telling it.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: The contest is narrative distribution, not legislation; media and creator platforms are where the pro-capital coalition is won or lost.
insights.quote: I don't see these as right versus left battles. I see these as narratives for winning the rising generation.

insights.claim: Salam's 'the real hero is Mark Zuckerberg's dad' framing argues the scarce input in America is not founders but the patient wealth-builders one generation back — dentists who make it possible for a child to attend a great school and own a computer.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: A reframing of household wealth accumulation as intergenerational infrastructure rather than consumption — the case for long-duration, boring compounding.
insights.quote: the real hero is not Mark Zuckerberg, it's Mark Zuckerberg's dad

insights.claim: Salam identifies resentment and envy as genuinely powerful motivators that political movements can monetize, but argues the compounding effect of patient reps and building beats them over time — and notes there is currently a lucrative business in selling people the victim message.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: A read on the attention economy: grievance content is a profitable business model, which is why it scales faster than build-oriented content.
insights.quote: Envy is a powerful drug. But an even more powerful drug is that thing that you get from getting reps and building something patiently over time.

insights.claim: Salam connects the current wave of anti-Israel radicalism to a broader resentment of visible wealth, power and achievement — arguing the fixation on a foreign policy issue is a symptom of people who feel bereft and unattached to anything larger than themselves.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Frames the movement's foreign-policy fixation as downstream of domestic economic alienation — meaning it moves with domestic conditions, not events abroad.

insights.claim: Assimilation is a two-way street in which immigrants adopt local norms and natives partly adopt immigrant norms — so norm enforcement matters: an immigrant arriving when fare evasion is punished assimilates to paying, and one arriving when everyone jumps the turnstile assimilates to that instead.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: A concrete mechanism linking visible enforcement of small infractions to long-run social outcomes — the operational case for broken-windows policing.
insights.quote: if you just see everyone else paying the fair when they get on the subway, you assimilate to that norm

insights.claim: Immigration, not gentrification, was the main driver of New York City's neighborhood revival through the 1980s, 1990s and 2000s: poor immigrants moved into neighborhoods abandoned by middle-class and working-class flight and their economic activity made those neighborhoods safer and better for residents already there.
insights.speaker: Reihan Salam
insights.so_what: Reframes the gentrification debate with a mechanism that argues for immigration-driven neighborhood investment as an asset-value tailwind, distinct from the current illegal-immigration disorder complaint.
